content.title: About
content.content: Buckwheat groats are the whole seeds of the buckwheat plant (Fagopyrum esculentum), cultivated in temperate regions of Europe and Asia. The groats have a distinct nutty flavor and a light, fluffy texture when cooked, and are used in dishes ranging from porridges to salads.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Buckwheat is not a true cereal but a pseudocereal, like quinoa.
It contains more rutin than most other grains, which supports vascular health.
Buckwheat was one of the first crops grown in China over 7,000 years ago.
In Russia, buckwheat is a traditional winter staple, often served as a simple boiled porridge.
Buckwheat seeds are pressed to produce buckwheat oil, rich in linoleic acid.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Buckwheat provides about 13 % protein, including all essential amino acids, making it a valuable plant‑based protein source.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Consuming buckwheat helps maintain stable blood‑sugar levels, beneficial for people with pre‑diabetes.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber in buckwheat supports digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Mineral source
items.content: Buckwheat is a good source of magnesium, iron, zinc, and manganese, important for metabolism and immunity.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Flavonoids such as rutin protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience an allergic reaction to buckwheat.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce the absorption of certain minerals; soaking the groats before cooking is recommended.

items.title: Possible contaminants
items.content: As with other grains, buckwheat may contain pesticide residues; choosing organic varieties is advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook buckwheat groats in a 1:2.5 ratio (groats:water) for 15‑20 minutes until tender. They can be served as a side dish, added to salads, casseroles, soups, or prepared as a porridge with milk and fruit. The groats can also be ground into buckwheat flour for gluten‑free baking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store buckwheat groats in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For long‑term storage, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent mold growth and preserve aroma.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-cheese-.title: Egg omelet or scrambled egg with cheese, tomatoes, and dark‑green vegetables, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of eggs, low‑fat cheese, fresh tomatoes and dark‑green vegetables (such as spinach or broccoli). It is prepared without added oil or other fats, making it a low‑calorie source of protein and valuable micronutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs provide a complete set of essential amino acids.
Dark‑green vegetables are rich in lutein and zeaxanthin, which support eye health.
Low‑fat cheese adds calcium and vitamin D while keeping fat content low.
Tomatoes contain lycopene – a powerful antioxidant that becomes more bioavailable after cooking.
The meal can be cooked on a dry pan or in the microwave, using the moisture released by the eggs.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Eggs provide about 6 g of protein per serving, helping maintain muscle mass.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and cheese supply vitamin B12, riboflavin and niacin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Bone support
items.content: Calcium from cheese and vitamin K from green vegetables contribute to bone mineralization.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Lycopene from tomatoes and carotenoids from green vegetables help neutralize free radicals.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: The absence of added fat makes the dish suitable for calorie‑restricted diets.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg white proteins.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Eggs contain cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Sodium in cheese
items.content: Low‑fat cheese can still be salty; choose reduced‑sodium options if you have hypertension.

items.title: Foodborne infection
items.content: Eggs should be fully cooked to avoid the risk of salmonella.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Beat the eggs with a splash of water, then stir in diced tomatoes, green vegetables and grated low‑fat cheese. Pour the mixture onto a pre‑heated dry skillet and cook over medium heat, stirring until the eggs set but remain tender. Alternatively, microwave for 1‑2 minutes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The dish is best eaten fresh. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat gently and add a little water to restore moisture.

hot-chocolate-cocoa-reduced-sugar-made-w.title: Hot chocolate / cocoa, reduced sugar, made with low‑fat (1 %) or fat‑free (skim) milk

content.title: About
content.content: Reduced‑sugar hot chocolate is made from cocoa powder, a modest amount of sweetener, and low‑fat (1 %) or fat‑free (skim) milk. The drink retains a rich chocolate flavor while containing fewer calories and less sugar than traditional hot chocolate.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cocoa powder is high in flavonoids, which have antioxidant properties.
Lower sugar helps better control blood glucose levels.
Low‑fat milk keeps most of the protein and calcium while contributing almost no fat.
Traditional hot chocolate is often prepared with whole milk, increasing its calorie content.
In many countries hot chocolate is a comforting winter beverage, while in others it is a popular café offering.

items.title: Rich in flavonoids
items.content: Flavonoids from cocoa may support cardiovascular health and improve blood flow.

items.title: Reduced sugar content
items.content: Less sugar lowers the risk of tooth decay and helps maintain stable energy levels.

items.title: Source of calcium and protein
items.content: Skim or low‑fat milk provides a significant portion of daily calcium and high‑quality protein.

items.title: Mood‑boosting compounds
items.content: Cocoa contains small amounts of theobromine, which can positively affect mood.

items.title: Lower calorie count
items.content: Reduced sugar and minimal fat make this beverage less caloric than classic hot chocolate.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy should use a dairy‑free alternative.

items.title: Caffeine content
items.content: Cocoa contains modest amounts of caffeine and theobromine, which may be undesirable in large amounts for sensitive individuals.

items.title: Sweetener side effects
items.content: Some sugar substitutes can cause gastrointestinal discomfort if consumed in excess.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the milk, whisk in cocoa powder and sweetener until smooth. Optionally top with sugar‑free whipped cream, a sprinkle of cinnamon, or a pinch of sea salt to enhance flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cocoa powder in an airtight container in a cool, dry place, and keep the prepared drink refrigerated for no more than 24 hours. Reheat to the desired temperature before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Shrimp and vegetables is a dish that combines seafood with fresh vegetables such as carrots, broccoli, and dark‑green leafy greens (spinach, kale). It is prepared without potatoes or soy‑based sauce, making it suitable for those avoiding gluten and soy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Shrimp are high‑protein and low‑calorie, popular in many diet plans.
Broccoli contains sulforaphane, a compound known for its antioxidant properties.
Dark‑green leafy greens like spinach are rich in iron and vitamin K.
Carrots are an excellent source of beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
The dish can be easily adapted to various cuisines by changing spices and cooking methods.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Shrimp provide high‑quality marine protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Supports eye health
items.content: Beta‑carotene from carrots converts to vitamin A, important for vision.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Broccoli and leafy greens supply vitamins C, E and polyphenols that combat free radicals.

items.title: Bone health
items.content: Vitamin K and calcium from leafy greens help strengthen bone tissue.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: The blend of vitamins and minerals in the dish boosts the immune system.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to shrimp, ranging from skin rash to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Shrimp contain cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should monitor portion size.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: If the vegetables are not organic, they may carry pesticide residues; thorough washing is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot as a main course or chill it for salads. Shrimp are best cooked by steaming, grilling, or quick sautéing to retain tenderness. Vegetables can be lightly blanched or steamed to keep crunch and nutrients.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Do not freeze together with leafy greens, as they may lose texture.

content.title: About
content.content: Tangerine (Citrus reticulata) is a citrus fruit native to Southeast Asia. It is smaller than an orange, easy to peel, and has a sweet-tart flavor with a bright aroma. Tangerines are eaten fresh, added to salads, desserts, and baked goods, made into juice, and their fragrant zest is used as a seasoning.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word tangerine comes from the name of the Moroccan city of Tangier.
In many countries of the former USSR, tangerines are a traditional symbol of the New Year.
Clementines and satsumas are close varieties of mandarin that are usually almost seedless.
The tangerine's skin is loose and easily separates from the flesh.
Tangerine zest is used in cooking, and dried peel is used in teas and spices.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and skin.

items.title: Contains fiber
items.content: Fiber, especially in the white strands on the segments, supports digestion.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate plays a role in cell formation.

items.title: Contains carotenoids
items.content: Beta-cryptoxanthin and other carotenoids give the fruit its color and have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Contains flavonoids
items.content: Hesperidin and other citrus flavonoids are studied as beneficial antioxidants.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Tangerines are acidic and may cause heartburn or irritate tooth enamel.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Citrus fruits can cause allergic reactions, especially in small children.

items.title: Juice and sugar
items.content: Tangerine juice has little fiber and a lot of sugar, so whole fruit is a better choice.

items.title: Medications
items.content: Unlike grapefruit, tangerines usually do not interfere with medications, but if a medication leaflet warns about citrus, consult a doctor.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Peel the tangerine and eat it in segments as a snack, or add it to salads, yogurt, desserts, and baked goods, or make sauces and drinks with it. The zest can be grated into dough, creams, and tea, but use thoroughly washed fruit for this.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Tangerines can be kept at room temperature for a few days, or in a cool place or the refrigerator for one to two weeks. Do not store them in tightly closed bags, as mold can develop. Discard any moldy fruit. The zest can be frozen.
